'''''Agrostis capillaris''''', the '''common bent''', '''colonial bent''', or '''browntop''', is a [[rhizomatous]] and [[stoloniferous]]  [[perennial]] in the grass family ([[Poaceae]]).  It is native to [[Eurasia]] and has been widely introduced in many parts of the world.<ref name=grass>{{cite web |url=http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Agrostis_capillaris&type=treatment |title=Grass Manual on the Web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611101709/http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Agrostis_capillaris&type=treatment |archive-date=11 June 2011 |access-date=15 March 2010}}</ref>  Colonial bent grows in moist [[grasslands]] and open [[meadows]], and can also be found in agricultural areas, roadsides, and invading disturbed areas.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?fr=1&sts=&lang=EN&si=1365 |title=Global Invasive Species Database: Ecology of ''Agrostis capillaris'' |publisher= Invasive Species Specialist Group|access-date=15 March 2010}}</ref>

The name ''[[Agrostis]]'' comes from the [[Greek language|Greek]] word meaning [[forage]] plant, ''agros'' meaning "a field".

It is found growing in neutral to acidic soils.  It has a very fine texture and like most bent grasses grows very dense. Although this species is used on golf courses, providing some of the best ball playing surfaces in the world, it also produces a spectacular visual appearance when maintained properly. It provides an excellent home lawn but is not tolerant of heavy use. Colonial bent is fairly easy to grow from seeds and fertilization of the lawn is not as intense.{{clarification needed|reason=not as intense as what?|date=November 2022}} This grass also takes longer to establish than creeping bent. However, it does not require the intense maintenance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://delta-intkey.com/grass/www/agrostis.htm |title=The grass genera of the world: descriptions, illustrations, identification, and information retrieval; including synonyms, morphology, anatomy, physiology, phytochemistry, cytology, classification, pathogens, world and local distribution, and references |access-date=19 August 2009 |last1=Watson |first1=L. |last2=Dallwitz |first2=M. J. |year=2008 |work=The Grass Genera of the World |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724221848/http://www.delta-intkey.com/grass/www/agrostis.htm |archive-date=24 July 2008 }}</ref>

Many internet sources describe it as being the tallest of the bent species.  However, C. E. Hubbard describes its height as ranging from 10 to 70 cm high, whereas the black bent ''[[Agrostis gigantea]]'' is 40 to 120 cm.  Marjorie Blamey, Richard and Alastair Fitter also describe black bent as being taller.<ref>{{cite book |title=Grasses |first=C. E. |last=Hubbard |date=1978 |publisher=Penguin}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland|first1=Marjorie |last1=Blamey |first2=Richard and Alistair |last2=Fitter|year=2003|publisher=A. & C. Black |isbn=0-7136-5944-0}}</ref>

==Description==
It forms a dense sward of fine leaves.  The [[ligule]] is short and does not come to a point.  This differs from creeping bent, ''[[Agrostis stolonifera]]'' in which it is pointed and up to 5mm long.

The flowering [[panicle]]s appear from May until June.  They are finely branched and look like a purple haze from a distance.  The panicle persists in winter after the seeds have been shed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |title=BSBI Description |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004923/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |archive-date=17 July 2011 |access-date=16 November 2010}}</ref>

==Environmental conservation==
''Agrostis capillaris'' forms a constituent of [[purple moor grass and rush pastures]], a type of Biodiversity Action Plan habitat in the UK. This habitat occurs on poorly drained neutral and acidic soils of the lowlands and upland fringe, and can be found in the south-west of England, especially in [[Devon]]. It is found on [[upland pastures]] throughout the UK.
